<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par135 />[but see Kittel; so 13:2, 6, 11; 10:26, but LXX {{GHGheb|text=מַצִּבַת}}], {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=36|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=6|verse=20}} (if the text is correct), 39:15 (read {{GHGheb|text=תֵּחָמֵם}} in v. 14), and to the plurals of names of animals, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=35|verse=7}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=11|verse=5}}. Conversely, plural suffixes refer to collective singulars, e.g. in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=16|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zp|chapter=2|verse=7}} [but read {{GHGheb|text=עַל הַיָּם}}]; and to a verbal idea contained in the preceding clause, in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=18}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=22|verse=21}} ({{GHGheb|text=בָּהֶם|translate=thereby}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=18|verse=26}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=33|verse=19|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGheb|text=עֲלֵיהֶם|translate=on that account, thereby}}).<ref>In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=7|verse=10}} for {{GHGheb|text=שֹׁעֵר}} (the LXX had {{GHGheb|text=שַׁ֫עַר}}) read {{GHGheb|text=שֹֽׁעֲרֵי}}.</ref> But the suffix in {{GHGheb|text=נְתָנוֹ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=21|verse=10}} refers to the collective idea contained in {{GHGheb|text=אֹֽיְבֶ֫יךָ}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jon|chapter=1|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=עִמָּהֶם}} refers to the sailors included in sense under the term {{GHGheb|text=אֳנִיָּה}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=2|verse=4}} read {{GHGheb|text=וַתִּצְפְּנֵם}}; in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=30|verse=6}} ({{GHGheb|text=מֵהֶם}}), 38:16, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=19|verse=5}} ({{GHGheb|text=בָּהֶם}}) the text is most probably corrupt.

{{GHGmargin-letter|135|q}}
3. In a few examples the force of the noun-suffix or possessive pronoun has become so weak that the language appears to be almost entirely unconscious of it. Thus in {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי|translate=my Lord}}, usually explained as being from the ''pluralis maiestatis'' {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנִים}} ({{GHGpar|124|i}}) with the suffix of the 1st singular (always with {{GHGterm|Qameṣ}} to distinguish it from {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנַי|translate=my lords}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=19|verse=2}}; but see note below), used exclusively of God, not only in addressing him ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=18|verse=3|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=35|verse=23}}), but ultimately (see, however, the note below), without any regard to the pronoun, as equivalent to ''the Lord''.<ref>Cf. the same weakening of the force of the possessive pronoun in {{GHGheb|text=רַבִּי}} prop. ''my master'', from the second century {{smaller|A.D.}} onwards ''the master''; so also in Syriac {{GHGheb|text=מרי|translate=my lord}}, and ultimately as a title ''the lord''; in Italian ''Madonna'', French ''Madame, Notre Dame, Monsieur, Monseigneur'', &c. It can, however, hardly be doubted that the regular distinction between {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי}} as a holy name, and {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנִי}} as an ordinary appellative is merely due to the practice of the later Rabbis. G. H. Dalman, ''Der Gottesname Adonaj und seine Geschichte'' (Berlin, 1889), in an exhaustive discussion, shows that apart from the book of Daniel and the eight critically doubtful passages, in which {{GHGheb|text=אדני}} is used by God himself, there is nowhere any necessity to regard the suffix as ''entirely'' meaningless, since {{GHGheb|text=אדני}} is always used either in an address ''to'' or (like {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנִי}}, which also is never a mere phrase or title) in reverent language ''about'' God—as the Lord of the speaker—like the Assyrian ''bēli-ia'', ''my lord''. Against any original distinction between {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי}} and {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנִי}} it may be urged especially that when unconnected with suffixes the singular {{GHGheb|text=אָדוֹן}} is always used of God, and not the ''pluralis maiestatis'' presupposed by {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי}}.</ref> On {{GHGheb|text=אֲדֹנָי}} as a ''Q<sup>e</sup>rê perpetuum'' of the Masoretes for {{GHGheb|text=יהוה}} see {{GHGpar|17|c}} and {{GHGpar|102|m}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|135|r}}
A similar loss of vitality in the suffix is generally assumed in {{GHGheb|text=יַחְדָּו}} prop. ''in his unitedness'', i.e. ''he'' &c. ''together'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־הָעָם יַחְדָּו}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=19|verse=8}}; then, without regard to the suffix, even after the 1st person {{GHGheb|text=אֲנַ֫חְנוּ יַחְדָּו}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=18}} in reference to two women; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=41|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=9|verse=32}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=6|verse=2}}, 7; after the 2nd person, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=45|verse=20}}, &c. But the supposed pronominal suffix is perhaps rather to be explained, with Brockelmann, {{GHGcite|title={{abbr|ZA.|Zeitschrift für Assyriologie und verwandte Gebiete, ed. by C. Bezold. Lpz. 18S6 ff.}}}} xiv. 344 f., as an old adverbial ending, which survives in the Arabic adverbs in ''u'' and in Assyrian.—Cf. further {{GHGheb|text=כֻּלָּם}} prop. ''their entirety'', but also after the 2nd person equivalent to ''all together'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=28}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=2}} (''hear, ye peoples, all of you''; cf. {{GHGpar|144|p}}), and even before the 2nd person, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=17|verse=10}} (in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=4}} read {{GHGheb|text=לָכֶם}} with the LXX).—On the redundant suffix in {{GHGheb|text=הָֽעֶרְכְּךָ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=27|verse=23}}, cf. {{GHGpar|127|i}}.<section end=par135 /><noinclude>
